Game basics

LineClash is a multiplayer falling-block game. Move and rotate each falling piece, build complete horizontal lines, and keep your stack below the top of the field. Cleared lines make room for more pieces and can earn attacks or specials, depending on the room rules.

Join your first game

Get a client for your platform, open the server browser, and select a server or add its host and port. Enter a nickname and password. When registration is enabled, a new nickname creates an account on that server. Reuse those credentials when returning to that server.

Choose a room and ready up. The room host starts the round and controls its rules and bots. Your nickname and statistics belong to that server; the same name elsewhere does not establish the same identity.

Read the playing field

Your field shows the active piece and its landing preview. Next shows the upcoming piece; Hold stores a piece for later when enabled. Hold is usable once per piece, then resets after a lock. Opponent boards show how the rest of the room is doing.

The specials inventory shows available items. Select an opponent or your own slot to use the next special when attacks are enabled. A topped-out player is eliminated and can watch the remaining players.

Reconnecting

During a connection loss, the game freezes locally and retries automatically while the server reserves your slot, normally for 15 seconds. Escape cancels recovery. A completed round, expired reservation, failed login or restarted server cannot restore the old active game. Updated clients restore the server’s authoritative board and active piece after reconnecting.

See controls, game modes and specials for the next steps.

How pieces, clears and levels work

Each piece is made of four blocks. Move it sideways and rotate it while it falls. Soft drop brings it down faster; hard drop places it immediately at the landing position. Once a piece locks, it becomes part of the stack and the next piece enters the field. A complete horizontal row clears, and the blocks above it move down. Leaving holes makes later clears harder; reaching the top can eliminate you.

The ghost outline previews a landing without placing the piece. Hold exchanges the active piece with the stored piece, or stores it and draws the next piece when Hold is empty. It is available only when the room enables it, and normally once between locks. Rotation can move a piece slightly around an obstruction when a supported wall kick fits; a blocked rotation simply fails.

Cleared lines contribute to your line count and progression. The starting level, lines required per increase and increase size are room settings. Faster levels reduce the time available to place pieces. Score, lines and survival describe different aspects of a round; the room's win condition determines its result.

Attacks and room rules

Rooms can enable specials, classic or guideline garbage, and different targeting rules. Garbage adds occupied rows and raises the stack. Guideline attack rules can reward combinations such as consecutive clears, back-to-back difficult clears and a perfect clear; configured bonuses vary by server. Learn the room's rules before comparing results across servers.

Specials are separate inventory items earned according to the room rules. Their effects can help you or disrupt opponents; choose the displayed target carefully. See specials for every effect. Long-running rounds can gain speed-up garbage when enabled, so a safe stack can become dangerous even without a new opponent attack.

Before starting, check the room settings, team name, player readiness and any bots. A paused game waits for play to resume; pause permissions depend on the room. A disconnected player has only the configured reconnect window to return. Elimination, voluntarily leaving and stopping the server are not ways to save a round for later.

Game modes

Multiplayer rooms

Up to eight participants can share a room. Room rules control hold, attacks, garbage targeting, speed-up and whether the last player wins. The host can configure the room before the round; server operators can restrict available features.

Practice with bots

Play alone or add easy, medium or hard AI opponents through the room’s AI controls. Bot and solo rounds are casual, making them useful for practicing placement and specials without affecting ranked wins.

Ranked and casual

A ranked round requires at least two humans, no active bots, and clients using the server-processed input protocol. The server simulates piece movement, gravity, holds, locks and clears, and derives awards from those results. Legacy board-reporting clients remain playable, but their rounds are casual. Stopped rounds are casual too.

Ranked results still depend on trusting the server operator. A legitimate protocol does not prevent account sharing, collusion or an operator fabricating reports. Casual rounds remain in match history.

Team play

Players on the same named team cooperate. Set or clear your team in the lobby. Team and individual results are displayed separately where supported by the server.

Spectating

Join as a spectator to watch without occupying a playing board, or continue watching after elimination. Spectators do not send gameplay inputs or earn a ranked win by observing.

Specials

Clear lines to earn specials when the room enables them. The inventory is ordered: using an item consumes the next available special. Number keys target the displayed player IDs; targeting yourself can be useful for defensive items.

Key Special Effect
a Add Line Adds garbage to the target field
c Clear Line Removes the bottom line
b Clear Specials Clears the target’s special inventory
r Random Clear Removes randomly selected blocks
o Block Bomb Clears blocks around a blast
q Quake Shifts rows sideways
g Gravity Pulls settled blocks downward
s Switch Field Exchanges settled boards with the target
n Nuke Clears the target field
i Immunity Temporarily protects against incoming specials
v Clear Column Clears a column
m Mutate Changes the active piece
d Darkness Temporarily obscures the target field
f Confusion Temporarily reverses movement and rotation controls

Effects depend on room rules and server implementation. In server-processed rounds, the server validates targets and inventory and applies board changes; clients cannot invent specials or award themselves clears. Turning attacks off disables special use.

Servers, match history and replays

Finding a server

Open Public servers in the native server browser, or copy an address from the website’s Servers page. Add the host and port, enter your nickname and password, and connect. Credentials are local to each server; do not assume the same nickname is the same person on different servers.

Use All, Favourites, Recent, Open slots or Ping ≤100 ms to narrow the native list. You can sort by latency or recent play. Unknown latency sorts last; an unknown capacity is not a promise of free slots. Favourite servers are saved locally, and recent entries are recorded after a successful connection.

Discovery does not send your account credentials to the directory. Selecting a new endpoint opens the connection form; saved credentials are reused only for the matching server and nickname.

Ranked and casual games

A round can award ranked wins when it starts with at least two human players, no active bots, and every player uses server-processed inputs. Older board-reporting clients play casual rounds. Manually stopped rounds, solo games and bot games are casual. Natural draws can count as ranked matches without awarding a winner. Ranked results are reported by the server; they are not a guarantee of tournament rules or cheat-free play.

Statistics includes match history, player records and ranked wins. Player records are scoped to the server and nickname. A placement of zero means unknown, such as after a disconnect. New timestamps use UTC; old history is labelled legacy rather than assigned a guessed timezone.

Watching a replay

Open a match from Statistics and choose its details or replay. Available replays support play/pause, seeking, playback speed and board snapshots. You can download the recorded events as JSON. Names link to the player’s history on that server.

A replay shows recorded gameplay snapshots rather than a frame-perfect video. Partial traces are labelled, and older matches may have no recording. Authentication and chat are excluded from recorded gameplay. A checksum detects damaged or changed data; it does not prove that a server operator reported an authentic game.
